title: Efficacy of surgical treatment in patients with trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis: A prospective study of 18 cases with evaluation of outcome and complications by independent evaluators
article_subtype: Prospective, consecutive surgical case series with independent assessment
condition_or_topic: Surgical treatment of trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis.
clinical_background: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, severe, unilateral pain attacks triggered by ordinarily harmless stimuli. Patients with multiple sclerosis have a 20-fold increased risk of developing trigeminal neuralgia. Demyelination affecting trigeminal pathways is considered a likely mechanism, although neurovascular contact with morphological changes may also contribute in some patients. Medical treatment can be difficult to tolerate and may worsen existing multiple sclerosis symptoms. Evidence on neurosurgical efficacy is limited: earlier studies reported complete pain relief without medication in 15–39% of patients after microvascular decompression, but relied on retrospective cohorts and lacked independent outcome assessment.
objectives: Assess pain-relief outcomes and complications after neurosurgical treatment of trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis in patients whose medical treatment had failed, using prospective follow-up and independent evaluators.
clinical_question: Patients: people with medically refractory trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis; interventions: microvascular decompression, glycerol rhizolysis or balloon compression; comparator: outcomes across the surgical procedures; outcomes: pain relief and surgical complications.
study_design: Prospective observational study that consecutively enrolled patients undergoing neurosurgery between May 2012 and October 2019. Clinical characteristics were collected before surgery, and a 3.0 Tesla MRI was assessed by a neuroradiologist blinded to the symptomatic side. Independent evaluators assessed outcomes and complications after surgery.

population.description: Patients with trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis (MS-TN) referred by a neurologist for neurosurgery after medical treatment had failed. Failure meant inadequate efficacy or intolerability of carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, or of the better tolerated of those two combined with gabapentin, lamotrigine or pregabalin. Diagnosis followed the applicable ICHD-2, ICHD-3 beta or ICHD-3 criteria at enrollment. The mean age was 54.6 years (range, 37 to 71).
inclusion_criteria: Diagnosis of MS-TN and neurosurgery after referral from a neurologist at the Danish Headache Center between May 2012 and October 2019.
Failure of medical treatment as defined by inadequate efficacy or intolerability.
For consideration of MVD, neurovascular contact on presurgical MRI.
exclusion_criteria: Incomplete one-year follow-up of surgical data.
More than 10% of clinical data missing for the analyses.
population.care_setting: Danish Headache Center, a tertiary centre for headache and facial pain treatment; neurosurgery was performed at the Department of Neurosurgery, Rigshospitalet, Denmark.

interventions: Microvascular decompression (MVD): a retrosigmoid craniectomy provided access to the trigeminal nerve. The implicated vessel was transposed where feasible or separated from the nerve with Teflon; a compressing vein could instead be coagulated and divided.

Balloon compression (BC): a neuronavigation-guided needle was passed through the foramen ovale, and a balloon was inflated with approximately 0.8 mL of Omnipaque under x-ray guidance to compress the trigeminal ganglion for two minutes.

Glycerol rhizolysis (GR): a needle was passed through the foramen ovale, 0.8 mL of glycerol was injected with the bed head elevated to 90 degrees, and the patient remained seated with the head slightly flexed for one hour.
comparators: Outcomes following MVD were compared descriptively with outcomes following the percutaneous procedures BC and GR.

primary: Pain relief measured with a modified seven-point Barrow Neurological Institute Scale (BNI): I denoted no pain or medication and an excellent outcome; II, IIIA and IIIB denoted good outcomes with differing pain and medication requirements; IV denoted a poor outcome; and VA and VB denoted treatment failure.
secondary: Surgical complications classified by a predefined protocol as major or minor, and as transient if lasting less than 12 months or permanent if present at the 12 months follow-up.
Medication use, medical adverse effects and pain intensity recorded during follow-up.

statistical_methods: Continuous and ranked variables were summarized descriptively; categorical variables were presented as frequencies (N, %). Reporting included numbers, means, percentages and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Missing data were treated as missing at random. P-values were two-tailed, with a significance level of 5%. Analyses used SAS 9.4, and reporting followed STROBE guidelines.
follow_up: Independent assessments took place at three, six and 12 months after surgery. At 12 months, patients also received a self-completed questionnaire. When questionnaire responses differed from the clinical follow-up record, the clinical record was used. For patients with multiple operations, follow-up data from the first procedure were reported.
interpretation: At one year, 64% of patients undergoing percutaneous procedures and 71% undergoing MVD had a good or excellent outcome. Major complications were more frequent and generally more serious after MVD. Both patients with neurovascular contact accompanied by morphological changes had an excellent 12-month outcome after MVD, which the authors regard as strong evidence that this finding may predict an excellent response in MS-TN. They suggest that neurovascular contact contributes less to MS-TN than to classical or idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia. Among patients with concomitant continuous pain, more than half had a good or excellent outcome, but the small cohort prevents conclusions about its influence on surgical response. TN duration tended to be shorter among patients with poor outcomes or treatment failure, without a significant difference in mean disease duration.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors report lower rates of excellent outcome after MVD in MS-TN than those reported for classical and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia. A prior study from their centre, using the same methodology in idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia with simple neurovascular contact and classical trigeminal neuralgia, found morphological changes highly predictive of an excellent MVD outcome and reported such an outcome in 70% of patients. Earlier MS-TN studies reported excellent outcomes after MVD in 15–39%; one study of 15 patients reported three patients (20%) at a mean follow-up of 88.2 months, without independent assessment or complication reporting. Truini et al. identified ipsilateral neurovascular contact with morphological changes alongside a demyelinating plaque in 17 of 28 patients, whereas a previous study from the authors’ group found no association between such contact and the symptomatic side. Prior reports of MVD complications in MS-TN differed: Broggi et al. reported complications in 6% of 35 patients, while Paulo et al. reported major complications in 38% of 24 patients, closer to the present findings. The authors consider MVD-related complications generally more frequent in MS-TN than in classical and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia, while noting that the evidence comes from few studies. In retrospective research on percutaneous procedures, Noorani et al. reported excellent outcomes after BC in 56% and after GR in 48% of patients; Mohammadi-Mohammadi et al. reported good outcomes in 39% after BC and 49% after GR, with complication rates of 25% and 16%, respectively. Studies of diffusion tensor imaging cited by the authors suggest that microstructural abnormalities in the cisternal trigeminal nerve segment may predict a good MVD outcome in MS-TN, although this imaging is not routinely performed in most clinical centres.
clinical_implications: Neurovascular contact with morphological changes on the symptomatic side may identify the subgroup of patients with MS-TN most likely to obtain an excellent outcome from MVD.
Although MVD can relieve pain in MS-TN, its risk of major complications must be considered; the authors judge outcomes and complication rates after percutaneous procedures acceptable.
The available cohort does not establish whether concomitant continuous pain or disease duration significantly affects surgical outcome.
practice_implications: The authors propose percutaneous procedures as the first-choice surgical approach for the majority of patients with MS-TN who require surgery.
MVD should be considered only when neurovascular contact with morphological changes is present on the relevant side.
limitations: The small sample size prevents firm conclusions about the effects of concomitant continuous pain or disease duration on surgical outcome.
Follow-up ended at 12 months after surgery, whereas other studies report longer follow-up.

The BNI scale has not been validated. The modified version captures pain relief and medication use but not other important outcomes, including pain intensity and physical and emotional functioning; the modification also makes comparisons between studies more difficult.
strengths: The prospective design and systematic assessment of surgical outcomes and complications by independent evaluators probably reduce evaluation bias.
open_questions: Whether concomitant continuous pain or disease duration significantly influences surgical outcome in MS-TN remains unresolved.
The authors question whether hypoesthesia after glycerol injection should be classified as a complication, given a cited study associating it with longer pain relief.
future_directions: Future studies should consider whether hypoesthesia ought to count as a complication.
The authors call for a well-defined set of core outcomes for future neurosurgical studies of trigeminal neuralgia.
The authors describe diffusion tensor imaging of trigeminal microstructure as a proposed presurgical prognostic method that could potentially improve surgical success in MS-TN.

safety_results.related_deaths: One patient (14%) in the MVD group died from a complication attributed to surgery. Patient no. 11 developed a posterior-fossa subdural hematoma within hours of surgery; an emergency re-operation removed it incompletely, and the patient died a few hours postoperatively.
notable_adverse_events: Major complications occurred in three patients (43%) after MVD, including the patient who died.
Minor complications occurred in two patients (29%) after MVD: transient hypoesthesia and transient hearing impairment.
Two patients (29%) had no surgical complications after MVD.

Patient no. 2, treated with MVD, had three separately assessed major complications: postoperative meningitis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis detected 35 days postoperatively, and CSF leakage with oto- and rhinoliquorrhea identified 12 months after surgery.
Patient no. 6, treated with MVD, had a symptomatic mesencephalic ischaemic stroke on day one postoperatively, with permanent dysarthria, ataxia and diplopia attributed to the stroke.
Patient no. 11, treated with MVD, had a fatal posterior-fossa subdural hematoma considered a surgical complication.
One patient underwent re-operation because postoperative MRI showed displacement of the inserted Teflon; the study did not classify this as a surgical complication.
Major complications occurred in three patients (27%) treated with percutaneous procedures.
Persistent hypoesthesia at the 12-month follow-up was classified as a major complication in two patients (33%) after BC.
Four patients (67%) had no complications attributed to BC.
Hypoesthesia at the 12-month follow-up was classified as a major complication in one patient (20%) after GR.
Transient hypoesthesia occurred in one patient (20%) after GR.
Three patients (60%) had no complications attributed to GR.

subgroup_analyses: Among the seven patients treated with MVD, the two with presurgical NVC accompanied by morphological changes on the symptomatic side both had an excellent 12-month outcome.

Concomitant continuous pain was present in five of the 18 patients. Of these, one patient with NVC and morphological changes had an excellent outcome after MVD; among three treated with GR, two had a good outcome and one had treatment failure; the remaining patient died after MVD.

Mean TN duration was 8.8 years in patients with an excellent or good outcome and 5.5 years in those with a poor, failed or fatal outcome. The difference between mean disease durations was not significant; no p-value was reported.

Mean MS duration was 14.9 years in patients with an excellent or good outcome and 17.8 years in those with a poor, failed or fatal outcome. The authors could not determine from this small cohort whether disease duration or concomitant continuous pain significantly affected surgical outcome.
secondary_results: The study included 18 patients: 11 women (61%) and seven men (39%). Mean age was 54.6 years (range, 37 to 71), and mean age at TN onset was 46.3 years (range, 36 to 57 years).
Mean TN duration was 7.7 years (range, 0 to 27 years), and mean MS duration was 15.9 years (range, 0 to 29 years).
Pain was left-sided in 12 patients, right-sided in five and bilateral in one.
Seven patients (39%) underwent MVD, six patients (33%) underwent BC and five patients (28%) underwent GR.

main_conclusion: The authors propose percutaneous procedures as the first surgical option for the majority of patients with MS-TN. They consider MVD effective in the subgroup with neurovascular contact accompanied by morphological changes, but emphasize its substantial risk of major complications and recommend considering it only for that subgroup.
narrative_summary:
This prospective study examined surgical outcomes and complications in 18 patients with trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis whose medical treatment had failed. Patients underwent MVD, BC or GR and were assessed by independent evaluators at three, six and 12 months. Presurgical assessment included 3.0 Tesla MRI, and pain relief was classified with a modified BNI scale.

Among seven patients who received MVD, two (29%) had an excellent outcome, three (43%) had a good outcome, one (14%) had treatment failure and one (14%) died following a surgical complication. Both excellent outcomes occurred in patients with neurovascular contact and morphological changes on the symptomatic side. Major complications affected three MVD patients (43%). Among 11 patients treated with a percutaneous procedure, seven (64%) had an excellent or good outcome; three (27%) had major complications. The authors report that major complications after MVD were more frequent and generally more serious than after percutaneous treatment.

For surgical decision-making, the authors propose percutaneous procedures for the majority of patients with MS-TN and restrict consideration of MVD to those with neurovascular contact accompanied by morphological changes. They caution that the small sample and follow-up limited to 12 months constrain interpretation. They also state that the modified BNI scale makes comparisons across studies more difficult.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Medical treatment of trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis has limited efficacy and tolerability, while evidence for neurosurgery is scarce. The study assessed surgical outcomes and complications. Patients undergoing microvascular decompression, glycerol rhizolysis or balloon compression were enrolled prospectively and consecutively from 2012 to 2019. Clinical characteristics and a 3.0 Tesla MRI were obtained before surgery; independent assessors conducted follow-up at three, six and 12 months. Among 18 patients, seven underwent microvascular decompression: two (29%) had an excellent outcome, three (43%) a good outcome, one (14%) treatment failure and one (14%) a fatal outcome. Both patients with excellent outcomes had neurovascular contact with morphological changes. Three patients (43%) had major complications. Among 11 patients undergoing percutaneous procedures, seven (64%) had excellent or good outcomes and three (27%) had major complications. The authors consider percutaneous outcomes and complication rates acceptable and recommend offering these procedures to the majority of patients who require surgery. They find microvascular decompression less effective and associated with more complications in this population than in classical and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia, and advise considering it only when neurovascular contact has produced morphological changes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Trigeminal neuralgia and multiple sclerosis are chronic neurological disorders that impair quality of life; multiple sclerosis is a central nervous system disorder that frequently causes disability in young adults. Trigeminal neuralgia causes severe, unilateral, electric shock-like episodes in one or more trigeminal branches, provoked by innocuous sensory stimuli and lasting at most two minutes. MRI findings distinguish idiopathic, classical and secondary trigeminal neuralgia. Classical disease requires ipsilateral neurovascular contact with morphological nerve changes; idiopathic disease has no contact or contact without morphological changes, termed simple contact, which also occurs commonly in healthy people. Intracranial conditions such as multiple sclerosis or a space-occupying lesion cause secondary disease. Multiple sclerosis involves autoimmune demyelination, inflammation and neurodegeneration. Compared with the background population, people with multiple sclerosis have a 20-fold greater risk of trigeminal neuralgia. Focal demyelination at the root entry zone, where oligodendroglial and Schwann-cell myelination meet, is proposed as a mechanism across causes of trigeminal neuralgia. In multiple sclerosis-associated disease, a pontine plaque is considered the most likely source of trigeminal afferent demyelination. A prospective MRI study by Truini et al. proposed a dual mechanism involving ipsilateral intrapontine demyelination and neurovascular contact with morphological changes; a recent MRI study by the present research group found the latter finding uncommon rather than a prevalent dual mechanism. Disease causation and treatment remain incompletely understood. Earlier microvascular decompression studies reported complete freedom from pain without medication in 15–39% of patients with multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia, but used retrospective cohorts, lacked independent assessment and did not prespecify outcomes. Because high-quality evidence is lacking, treatment follows guidance for idiopathic and classical disease. The European Academy of Neurology recommends carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine as first-choice medical treatments for those conditions; if they are ineffective, lamotrigine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin type A, pregabalin, baclofen or phenytoin may be considered. For medically refractory classical disease, microvascular decompression is the first-choice operation. Guidance does not favor a particular operation for idiopathic disease with neurovascular contact, whereas neuroablative methods are recommended when contact is absent. Those methods include gamma knife surgery, glycerol rhizolysis, balloon compression and radiofrequency thermocoagulation; on low-quality evidence, they are considered similarly effective. Evidence specific to secondary disease is sparse, and better data are needed to compare surgical outcomes across disease types. Drug adverse effects, including tiredness and ataxia, make treatment poorly tolerated in multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia and may worsen existing multiple sclerosis symptoms, so surgery is often considered. The authors aimed to prospectively assess surgical efficacy in medically refractory patients using independent evaluators.

document_sections.heading: Methods Definition of the cohort and baseline characteristics
document_sections.content: The investigators prospectively enrolled consecutive patients diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis who underwent neurosurgery after referral by a neurologist at the Danish Headache Center, a tertiary headache and facial-pain treatment center, between May 2012 and October 2019. Depending on enrollment date, diagnosis followed ICHD-2, ICHD-3 beta or ICHD-3 criteria. Patients were excluded for incomplete one-year surgical follow-up or inability to give informed consent. After referral, a neurologist conducted a clinical interview and neurological examination. A semi-structured interview recorded demographics, clinical features, present and previous medical and surgical treatments, comorbidities and sensory deficits. Data collection largely followed the group's earlier studies of classical, idiopathic and secondary trigeminal neuralgia. Referral for neurosurgery required failed medical treatment, defined as inadequate efficacy or intolerability of carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, or of the better of those two combined with gabapentin, lamotrigine or pregabalin. Microvascular decompression was considered only when neurovascular contact was present.

document_sections.heading: Presurgical neuroimaging
document_sections.content: Every patient underwent 3.0 Tesla MRI within eight weeks of the clinical interview. An experienced neuroradiologist assessed the scans without knowing the symptomatic side. Imaging used a 3.0 Tesla Phillips Achieva system with a 32-channel head coil and Multi Transmit parallel RF transmission. The protocol included whole-brain sagittal T2-weighted turbo-spin-echo imaging, T2-weighted DRIVE SPIR, 3D time of flight MR angiography (s3DI MC HR) and high-spatial-resolution, heavily T2-weighted 3D balanced fast field echo [BFFE]. Multiplanar views of the cisternal nerve were reconstructed parallel to the trigeminal nerve in axial and sagittal planes and perpendicular to it in the coronal plane. Neurovascular contact meant that a vessel touched the nerve with no visible intervening cerebrospinal fluid; uncertain contact was classified as absent. Contact was categorized according to whether it caused morphological changes, defined as compression, displacement, indentation, distortion or atrophy. Pontine plaques were considered relevant when they lay along intrapontine trigeminal afferents in the ventrolateral pons, including the pontine trigeminal nuclei. The protocol did not cover trigeminal nuclei in the medulla oblongata or spinal medulla. Postoperative imaging was obtained only when clinically indicated.

document_sections.heading: Neurosurgical technique
document_sections.content: Specialized, highly experienced neurosurgeons performed microvascular decompression, balloon compression and glycerol rhizolysis at the Department of Neurosurgery, Rigshospitalet, Denmark.

document_sections.heading: Microvascular decompression.
document_sections.content: The procedure followed the group's previously published approach for classical and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia and was considered only after presurgical MRI showed neurovascular contact. Surgeons used a supracerebellar infratentorial route through a retrosigmoid craniectomy, without retractors, specific relaxation techniques, neuronavigation, brainstem auditory evoked responses or other neuromonitoring. They exposed the cerebellopontine angle and identified the nerve and compressing vessel. For superior cerebellar artery compression, they preferred to move the artery upward and secure it to the tentorium with Teflon and glue; if that was not possible, they placed Teflon between vessel and nerve. They used interposition for contact with the anterior inferior cerebellar artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery. A compressing vein was moved and secured with Teflon and glue, or coagulated and divided to prevent avulsion.

document_sections.heading: Balloon compression.
document_sections.content: With the patient supine and the head extended, surgeons used Brain Lab neuronavigation to guide a needle from the skin near the mouth corner on the symptomatic side through the oval foramen. After removing the stylet, they inserted a balloon and inflated it under x-ray guidance with approximately 0.8 mL of Omnipaque. A balloon shape matching Meckel’s cave confirmed its position. They compressed the trigeminal ganglion for two minutes before removing the balloon and needle.

document_sections.heading: Glycerol rhizolysis.
document_sections.content: With the patient supine and the head extended, surgeons passed a needle through the foramen ovale as described for balloon compression. They then raised the head of the bed to 90 degrees and injected 0.8 mL of glycerol. The patient's head was slightly flexed and supported in the seated position for one hour to keep as much glycerol as possible within Meckel’s cave.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: A neurologist at the Danish Headache Center assessed patients at three, six and 12 months after surgery using a purpose-built form covering the seven-point Barrow Neurological Institute Scale (BNI), surgical complications, medication, medication adverse effects and pain intensity. At the 12-month visit, patients also received a self-completed questionnaire translated and slightly modified by the investigators. When questionnaire and clinical-form data differed, the clinical-form information took precedence. For patients with more than one operation, the reported follow-up concerned the first procedure. A prespecified protocol classified surgical complications as major or minor. Major complications comprised death; ischaemic or haemorrhagic cerebellar or brainstem stroke; anaesthesia dolorosa; meningitis; cerebrospinal fluid leakage; hydrocephalus; permanent ataxia or diplopia; corneal keratitis; permanent severe hypoesthesia; permanent facial nerve palsy; and permanent hearing loss or impairment. When a surgical stroke caused cranial nerve dysfunction, dizziness or ataxia, those manifestations were not counted as additional complications. Events lasting less than 12 months were transient; those still present at the 12 months follow-up were permanent. Minor complications comprised dizziness, tinnitus, tiredness, wound infection, headache, scar discomfort, transient ataxia or diplopia, reduced or absent corneal reflex, permanent mild hypoesthesia, transient mild or severe hypoesthesia, trigeminal motor weakness affecting the masseter, transient facial nerve palsy, transient hearing loss or impairment, and altered taste.

document_sections.heading: Outcome
document_sections.content: The primary outcome was pain relief measured with a modified BNI scale intended to distinguish surgical outcomes more finely. Category I meant no pain and no medication and constituted an excellent outcome. Category II meant occasional pain without a need for medication and was a good outcome. IIIA meant no pain while taking daily medication and was good; IIIB meant occasional pain adequately controlled by medication and was also good. IV denoted reduced pain that medication did not adequately control and was poor. VA denoted no pain relief, and VB worsening pain; both were failures.

document_sections.heading: Statistical analyses
document_sections.content: Continuous and ranked variables were summarized descriptively, while categorical variables were presented as frequency distributions (N, %). Results were reported as numbers, means and percentages, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Patients were excluded from analysis if more than 10% of clinical data were missing; missingness was assumed to be random. P-values were two-tailed, with a 5% significance threshold. Analyses used SAS 9.4, and reporting followed STROBE guidelines.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The study included 18 patients: 11 women (61%) and seven men (39%). Mean age was 54.6 years (range, 37 to 71), and mean age at trigeminal neuralgia onset was 46.3 years (range, 36 to 57 years). Mean trigeminal neuralgia duration was 7.7 years (range, 0 to 27 years); mean multiple sclerosis duration was 15.9 years (range, 0 to 29 years). Pain was left-sided in 12 patients, right-sided in five and bilateral in one. Seven patients (39%) underwent microvascular decompression, six (33%) balloon compression and five (28%) glycerol rhizolysis. The inclusion flowchart covers 859 patients with trigeminal neuralgia in the research database from May 2012 to October 2019: 736 were excluded for classical or idiopathic disease, 27 for secondary disease due to causes other than multiple sclerosis and 14 for lack of informed consent. Among the remaining patients, 61 received medical treatment and 21 underwent surgery; 3 surgical patients were excluded because of missing data, leaving 18 for this study. Table 1 presents individual baseline clinical characteristics.

document_sections.heading: Outcome
document_sections.content: Of seven patients undergoing microvascular decompression, two (29%) achieved an excellent outcome (BNI I), three (43%) a good outcome (BNI IIIA-IIIB), one (14%) treatment failure (BNI VA) and one (14%) a fatal outcome. The two excellent responders both had neurovascular contact with morphological changes on the symptomatic side on presurgical MRI. Of six balloon compression patients, one (17%) had an excellent outcome (BNI I), three (50%) a good outcome (BNI IIIA-IIIB), one (17%) a poor outcome (BNI IV) and one (17%) treatment failure (BNI VB) at 12-months follow-up. Among five glycerol rhizolysis patients, two (40%) had a good outcome (BNI IIIB), while three (60%) had treatment failure (BNI VA). Table 2 shows outcomes and complications by patient and follow-up time; recurrence requiring re-operation before 12 months was classified as failure, irrespective of the repeat procedure, whose results were not assessed. Five of the 18 patients had concomitant continuous pain. One had neurovascular contact with morphological changes and an excellent outcome after microvascular decompression. Three underwent glycerol rhizolysis, with two good outcomes and one treatment failure. The remaining patient died after microvascular decompression. Mean trigeminal neuralgia duration was 8.8 years among excellent or good responders and 5.5 years among patients with poor, failed or fatal outcomes. Corresponding mean multiple sclerosis durations were 14.9 years and 17.8 years. Differences between the disease-duration means were not significant.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Table 2 reports major and minor complications at 12 months follow-up. Complications following each surgical approach are described in the subsequent subsections.

document_sections.heading: Microvascular decompression.
document_sections.content: Three patients (43%) experienced major complications, including the fatal case. Two (29%) had minor complications, namely transient hypoesthesia or transient hearing impairment, and two (29%) had no surgical complications. One patient required another operation after postoperative MRI confirmed displacement of the inserted Teflon; the investigators did not classify this as a surgical complication. Patient no. 2 had three independently counted major complications: postoperative meningitis confirmed by spinal fluid sampling and treated with intravenous antibiotics and re-operation to cover a dural defect with TachoSil; cerebral venous sinus thrombosis confirmed by MRI 35 days after surgery, located in the internal jugular vein and treated with anticoagulation; and a cerebrospinal fluid fistula with oto- and rhinoliquorrhea confirmed 12 months after surgery, for which re-operation closed two intraoperatively identified dural defects. Patient no. 6 developed a symptomatic mesencephalic ischaemic stroke on postoperative day one. This patient had known protein S deficiency and permanent stroke-related dysarthria, ataxia and diplopia. Patient no. 11 died from a complication attributed to surgery: consciousness progressively declined a few hours after the operation, CT showed a posterior-fossa subdural hematoma, and urgent re-operation removed it only incompletely amid inadequate coagulation. Death occurred a few hours postoperatively.

document_sections.heading: Balloon compression and glycerol rhizolysis.
document_sections.content: After balloon compression, two of six patients (33%) still had hypoesthesia at 12-months follow-up, classified as major; four (67%) had no procedure-related complication. After glycerol rhizolysis, one patient (20%) had hypoesthesia at 12-month follow-up, classified as major, and one (20%) had transient hypoesthesia. The other three patients (60%) had no related complications.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors describe this as the first prospective, systematic follow-up of surgically treated patients with multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia using independent assessment of outcomes and complications after one year. Good or excellent outcomes occurred in 64% after percutaneous procedures versus 71% after microvascular decompression, but major complications were more frequent and generally more serious with microvascular decompression. Age at onset aligned with reports of earlier onset in this population, typically between 40 and 50 years. The article's graphical comparison also includes a previously published cohort of classical and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia patients with neurovascular contact treated by microvascular decompression (n=115); those are results of the earlier study, not additional patients in the present cohort.

document_sections.heading: Does diseases duration and concomitant continuous pain determine surgical outcome?
document_sections.content: Among five patients with concomitant continuous pain, three had good or excellent outcomes, one experienced treatment failure and one died. The excellent responder underwent microvascular decompression and had significant neurovascular contact. Thus, more than half had a clinically significant good or excellent outcome. Trigeminal neuralgia duration tended to be shorter among patients with poor outcomes or failure. Because the cohort was small, the authors could not establish whether concomitant continuous pain or disease duration significantly affected surgical outcome.

document_sections.heading: Outcome after microvascular decompression may be dependent on neurovascular contact
document_sections.content: In the present cohort, both patients with neurovascular contact causing morphological changes who underwent microvascular decompression had excellent outcomes at 12 months. The authors regard this as strong evidence suggesting that such contact predicts a favorable response to that operation in multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia. They consider neurovascular contact probably the principal cause in classical trigeminal neuralgia, in which many patients achieve excellent rather than merely good results after decompression. In an earlier study from their center using the same methods and assessing two-year results in idiopathic disease with simple contact and classical disease, morphological changes strongly predicted excellent results, which occurred in 70% of all patients. Earlier microvascular decompression studies in multiple sclerosis-associated disease have been inconsistent. One study followed 15 patients for a mean of 88.2 months and reported an excellent outcome in three (20%); it lacked independent assessment and complication reporting, and five patients underwent re-operation. Other retrospective studies reported excellent outcomes in 15-39%. Truini et al. found concurrent ipsilateral morphological neurovascular contact and a demyelinating plaque in 17 of 28 patients and considered contact important to causation. In contrast, the present authors' earlier research found no association between such contact and the symptomatic side. They consider the present findings consistent with that work, noting that only two patients undergoing microvascular decompression had contact with morphological changes. They interpret the lower excellent-response rates after decompression in multiple sclerosis-associated disease, relative to idiopathic and classical disease, as suggesting that neurovascular contact has a lesser causal role. They suggest performing decompression only when morphological neurovascular contact is present on the relevant side. Canadian diffusion tensor imaging studies suggested that microstructural abnormalities in the cisternal trigeminal segment, rather than the root entry or intrapontine segments, may predict a good decompression response. Presurgical diffusion tensor imaging might improve response prediction and potentially surgical success, but most clinical centers do not use it routinely. The authors know of no earlier surgical study in this population with independent complication assessors. Broggi et al. reported cerebrospinal fluid leakage and one facial nerve palsy case, with complications in 6% of 35 patients. Paulo et al. reported major complications, including aseptic meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid leakage and pseudomeningocele, in 38% of 24 patients, closer to the present findings. Taken together, the authors consider complications from decompression generally much more frequent in multiple sclerosis-associated disease than in classical or idiopathic disease, while cautioning that this conclusion rests on few studies.

document_sections.heading: Percutaneous procedures
document_sections.content: Percutaneous operations are used more often than microvascular decompression in multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia. In a retrospective study with mean follow-up of 25 months, Noorani et al. assessed 33 patients who underwent 64 percutaneous procedures and reported excellent outcomes in 56% after balloon compression and 48% after glycerol rhizolysis. Another retrospective study by Mohammadi-Mohammadi et al. covered 277 procedures in 96 patients: among 19 patients receiving balloon compression first, 39% had a good outcome after mean follow-up of 29 months; among 39 receiving glycerol rhizolysis, 49% had a good outcome after mean follow-up of 28 months. Reported complication rates were 25% after balloon compression and 16% after glycerol rhizolysis; most events, such as dysesthesia or reduced corneal reflex, were minor. The present study counted hypoesthesia as either a major or minor complication according to severity. Because a Danish neurosurgical study associated hypoesthesia after glycerol injection with longer pain relief, the authors suggest that future studies reconsider whether hypoesthesia should be classified as a complication.

document_sections.heading: Strengths and weaknesses
document_sections.content: Independent assessment of surgical outcomes and complications, together with prospective design, is identified as a major strength that probably reduces evaluation bias. The authors think this approach may also produce lower apparent efficacy and higher complication rates than retrospective studies without independent evaluation. Although BNI is widely used in neurosurgical trigeminal neuralgia research, it has not been validated. Their modified BNI is practical clinically but captures only pain-relief category and medication use, not other important outcomes such as pain intensity or physical and emotional functioning. The modification provides more outcome detail but limits comparison between studies. The authors call for a defined set of core trigeminal neuralgia outcomes for future surgical research. Follow-up ending at 12 months is a limitation relative to studies with longer observation, and the small sample is another important limitation.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that microvascular decompression can be effective for patients with multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia and morphological changes of the trigeminal nerve, but carries a high risk of major complications. They regard outcomes and surgical complication rates after percutaneous procedures as acceptable and comparable to microvascular decompression for classical and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia. They propose percutaneous procedures as the first surgical choice for the majority of patients with multiple sclerosis-associated disease and advise considering microvascular decompression only when neurovascular contact has produced morphological changes.

document_sections.heading: Article Highlights
document_sections.content: The article emphasizes lower efficacy and more complications with microvascular decompression in multiple sclerosis-associated trigeminal neuralgia, recommends percutaneous procedures as the first surgical choice, and limits its recommendation for microvascular decompression to patients with neurovascular contact and morphological changes.

document_sections.heading: Standard protocol approvals and patient consents
document_sections.content: The Danish National Committee on Health Research Ethics determined that ethical approval was unnecessary because the project was observational and relied on routine clinical care and laboratory assessment. All participants provided written informed consent under Danish Data Protection Agency regulations.
